content: There have been significant interventions aimed at preventing drug use and HIV transmission. Staff from four new organizations have been trained to deliver services related to drug use and HIV. District AIDS Councils have been established in selected districts to reduce stigma and engage both government and public sectors, thereby improving access to health, social welfare, and HIV-related services for clients of Nai Zindagi. However, challenges persist, including human resource shortages, ongoing stigma, discrimination, and harassment of people who inject drugs, particularly from law enforcement, which discourages the use of public sector services. Nai Zindagi is sharing its expertise and technical knowledge with programs in Nepal, Indonesia, and Kenya. In Tanzania, Médecins du Monde (MdM) provides comprehensive harm reduction services for people who use drugs, with a focus on women and enabling consistent engagement with care. These services include needle and syringe programs, referrals to opioid substitution therapy, income-generating activities, and legal assistance. MdM also builds the capacity of non-governmental and community-based organizations to run harm reduction services, such as drop-in centers, and encourages the establishment of dedicated centers and shelters for women, offering additional health and support services for their children. MdM has supported the creation of national and district-level harm reduction committees with representation from governmental and non-governmental institutions, which are responsible for resource mobilization and other activities. Dialogue with municipal, district, and national authorities, as well as sensitization sessions for police, health providers, and journalists, have been key to their work. Partnerships with all societal members are considered essential for scaling up harm reduction nationwide. Since 2011, over 6,000 people who use or inject drugs have received harm reduction services, and in 2013, more than 2,000 stakeholders were trained in harm reduction approaches and interventions. In Ukraine, harm reduction services led by NGOs under the International HIV/AIDS Alliance reached up to 23% of the estimated population of people who inject drugs by 2007. The introduction of Peer-Driven Interventions (PDI) in 2007 extended services to underserved groups, such as women and adolescents, by leveraging social networks and incentive-based recruitment. PDI also collects data to tailor services to specific sub-populations and has been used to reach sex workers and street children. Group-level interventions and couples counseling have facilitated outreach to young stimulant users and sexual partners of people who inject drugs. Pharmacies have been involved as secondary outlets for distributing injecting instruments and prevention commodities, increasing program coverage by up to 10% in some areas. Rapid HIV testing and case management approaches have reduced the time between HIV diagnosis and treatment enrollment. In Afghanistan, the Afghan Family Guidance Association (AFGA) provides comprehensive HIV prevention, treatment, and care services for female prisoners, focusing on harm reduction for drug users. Advocacy efforts have promoted gender-sensitive and rights-based approaches to reduce stigma and discrimination. Support groups for female prisoners and peer educators trained in harm reduction have been established. In Albania, the NGO STOP AIDS implemented an incentives program to encourage safer behaviors among young people who inject drugs. Participants earned vouchers redeemable for retail goods by engaging in harm reduction activities, such as obtaining clean needles, returning used ones, and undergoing HIV testing. The program significantly improved attendance and uptake of harm reduction services, though its impact on certain behaviors, such as adherence to opioid substitution therapy, was less pronounced. In Indonesia, methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) was piloted in Kerobokan Prison in Bali in 2005, leading to the establishment of harm reduction services in 11 other prisons and detention centers. The program has achieved high levels of integration with community health services, ensuring continuity of care for prisoners transitioning to the community. HIV testing and treatment have also been effectively implemented in prisons, with over 90% of high-risk prisoners tested and many starting antiretroviral therapy. In Iran, harm reduction strategies, particularly opioid substitution therapy with methadone, have been widely implemented following an HIV outbreak among prisoners in 1996. By 2014, over 4,000 drug treatment centers offered opioid substitution therapy, with most managed by private sector physicians. These efforts have significantly addressed the concentrated HIV epidemic driven by injecting drug use. In Cambodia, the SMARTgirl program provides HIV prevention and sexual and reproductive health services to entertainment workers, many of whom are sex workers. The program uses peer-led outreach to deliver information, commodities, and referrals, and supports harm reduction approaches for workers who inject drugs. SMARTgirl also works to reduce stigma and discrimination, reaching nearly half of all entertainment workers in Cambodia. In Ghana, the SHARPER project recruits young female sex workers as peer educators to increase service uptake and engagement in care. Peer educators receive training, supervision, and stipends, and work with small groups of sex workers to address priority issues such as safer sex negotiation, family planning, and violence prevention. The program also provides peer-accompanied referrals and links to critical support services. In Myanmar, the AIDS Myanmar Association (AMA) supports over 2,000 sex workers, focusing on capacity building and community mobilization to advocate for their health and human rights. AMA provides STI and HIV prevention tools, links to health facilities, and follow-up care in a supportive environment. In the Philippines, the River of Life (ROLi) program helps adolescent males who have sex with men assess and reduce their risk behaviors through self-assessment tools, workshops, and peer group work. The program serves 6,000 young people, most of whom live in poverty and engage in sex work and drug use. Outreach is conducted through peer-to-peer interactions, online platforms, and social media, providing opportunities for risk self-assessment and access to health services.
